title: Violetta alone
where: *La Traviata*, Act 1, Scenes 3 and 5, and the last lines of Act 3
about: Violetta Valery, a Paris courtesan, is the title’s *traviata*, the woman led astray. At a party in her house Alfredo Germont tells her he has loved her for a year; she has only friendship to give, she says, and hands him a flower to bring back the next day. The guests leave, and for the rest of the act she is alone on the stage. The third passage is the end of the opera: she is dying of consumption, with Alfredo, his father, her maid and the Doctor beside her.

view.says: Auden wrote no essay on this opera but took an example from its last scene. Opera, he held, is about human willfulness: people will have their feelings, cost what it may. What is sung is so, and a singer cannot be shown deceiving herself as a character in a play can. At most the orchestra may contradict the singer, as it does, he says, when Germont comes to Violetta’s deathbed.
view.quote: Self-deception is impossible in opera because music is immediate, not reflective; whatever is sung is the case.
view.source: “Notes on Music and Opera,” in *The Dyer’s Hand* (1962), pp. 470–71
view.checked: read in the scan of The Dyer’s Hand, research/auden/dh.txt, on 2026-10-03: lines 22121-22124 (p. 470: willfulness, the cost) and 22164-22185 (p. 471: the Mistake, self-deception, and the sentence that names La Traviata; the words quoted are lines 22178-22180). The running heads stand at the top of their pages (p. 470 at line 22110, p. 471 at line 22157). Germont comes in at the head of the last scene of the libretto. Also in remake/research/C_auden_on_works.md, section 33.

lenses.label: Refrain
lenses.name: refrain
lenses.plain: words that come back at a set place in a song or poem; here they were first sung by another voice
lenses.caption: Alfredo ends his declaration with four lines on what love is, hung from amor, love, the last word of the line before. Alone, Violetta says his words are scolpiti, carved, in her heart, and both stanzas of her slow song close on them. The first printing sets them deeper in than her own lines. Three lines return word for word; the first is refitted, and his l’anima, the soul, becomes palpito, heartbeat. Auden held that in opera self-deception cannot be sung, because what is sung is so. Her song bears her out: where she says what love is, the words are his. An early study says his tune returns too.
lenses.why: Piave closes both stanzas of Violetta’s song on Alfredo’s lines, so what she has just said, that his words are carved in her heart, is shown to be so; Auden held that in opera what is sung is so.

lenses.label: Measure
lenses.meterName: seven syllables by the Italian count: the last accent always on the sixth

points.say: A sliding ending: two unstressed syllables follow the last accent, so eight syllables are heard. Of the four lines this one alone has no rhyme.
The vowel that ends the first word runs into the vowel that begins the second, and the two count as one syllable.
The line stops on its last accent, so six syllables are heard. The line before the four ends the same way, and the two rhyme.
Her recitative, the sung speech before the song, begins with two lines of the same measure. Recitative mixes lines of seven and of eleven syllables freely.
Her eighth line ends as the line before his four did: cut short, on the word for love.

lenses.caption: By the Italian count every line here is a seven: its last accent falls on the sixth syllable, and eight, seven or six syllables are heard as two unstressed ones follow, or one, or none. Alfredo’s four go eight, seven, seven, six and stop on cor, heart, rhymed with amor, love. Violetta’s song is in the same measure and ends its eighth line on all’amor, to love, so his four lines close her stanza without a seam. The mixed endings mark the form that became the opera aria. Auden and Kallman wrote that a convention of forms, settled before Verdi’s middle years, assured the composer a text he could set.
lenses.why: Violetta’s song keeps Alfredo’s measure and reaches his rhyme word, so his lines close her stanza without a seam; it is the stock form of the opera aria, which gave the composer a text he could set.

grounds.claim: each of the twelve rows has its last stress on the sixth syllable; rows 1.0 and 5.0 end sliding (eight heard), rows 0.3, 1.3, 4.7 and 5.3 end on the stress (six heard), the rest end plainly (seven); 1.3 rhymes with 0.3 and 5.3 with 4.7; 1.1 with 1.2

lenses.caption: The four lines call love the soul (in her song, the heartbeat) of the whole universe, mysterious, altero, proud, and croce e delizia, cross and delight, to the heart. Torment and pleasure are joined by nothing more than e, and. Cor for heart and accenti for words are forms the dictionary marks as poetic, the old stock of libretto verse. The woman who repeats them is a courtesan, Auden’s own word for Violetta. He held that everybody has joyful, tender and noble feelings, and that opera can show it where spoken drama cannot: a song may come at the wrong moment, never from the wrong person.
lenses.why: Piave gives a courtesan the old poetic words for love as the heartbeat of the universe and a cross to the heart; Auden held that such feelings belong to everybody and that opera, unlike spoken drama, can show it.

lenses.label: English

ties.say: Both versions end this line on the word for love. Piave hangs the next four lines from it. The English ends its sentence here and begins another.
Piave’s line says what love is: the soul of the universe. The English says what the singer’s bosom did.
The whole universe is gone. A *chain* that surrounds comes in, which is not in the Italian.
One word is carried over whole, *mysterious*. In the English it describes the chain.
Two nouns joined by *and* are kept. The cross, a figure for torment, becomes *pain*.
Both versions end the four lines on the word for heart, one stressed syllable.
Piave’s word is *strano*, strange, said of what amazes and may also trouble. The English chooses *wondrous*. In the last scene it gives the same Italian word as *strange*.
Carved becomes *graven*. The English adds *seem*; in the Italian she says outright that she has the words carved in her heart.

lenses.caption: The English is from a New York libretto that names no translator. It keeps the frame: four lines that come back, and a last line that joins two nouns and stops on the word heart. Inside it the soul and the universe are gone, a chain comes in, the cross becomes pain, and three lines running rhyme on two syllables. Auden and Kallman wrote that the translation of an aria need give only its emotion. They also wrote that two-syllable rhymes, the commonest in Italian, are mostly comic in English, and that in a tender scene no rhyme is better than a laughable one.
lenses.why: The English keeps the frame of the four lines and replaces what they say; by Auden and Kallman’s account an aria’s translation owes only the emotion, yet its two-syllable rhymes are the kind they call mostly comic in English.

points.say: The question, what must I do, comes in a line of eleven syllables, the long line of recitative.
From here on every line has a stress on its third syllable and on its seventh.
Two vowels meet and count as one syllable.
The line stops on its last accent, so seven syllables are heard. The last line of the song stops the same way, and the two rhyme.
Every second syllable is stressed. The two verbs, be born and die, stand at the two ends of the line with the day twice between them: a crossing.

lenses.caption: The recitative, her sung speech before the song, ends in two lines of eleven syllables. Then the line turns to eight, stressed on the third and seventh syllables in all eight lines. It is an old line, used in dance songs, religious songs and carnival songs. The guests took their leave in it, with gioir, rejoicing, and piacer, pleasure, at line ends; gioire and piacer end lines here. A fast song that closes an aria is a cabaletta, and its effect lies in the even return of one rhythmic figure. Auden and Kallman say it is written to let the singer show her skill.
lenses.why: The song that chooses pleasure is in the eight-syllable line of the guests’ farewell, and two of their rhyme words end lines here; all eight lines are stressed alike, and a cabaletta’s effect lies in a rhythm that returns unchanged.

lenses.label: Rhyme
lenses.caption: Like her first recitative, this one closes on two lines that rhyme, and the rhyme joins gioire, to take joy, to finire, to end, a verb that can mean to die. Opera, Auden held, imitates human willfulness: people will have their feelings whatever it costs them. In the song, printed as two groups of four lines, rhyme ties the halves together, the second line to the fifth and the fourth to the eighth. As sung, six of the song’s eight lines have other words, and every rhyme is kept. For Auden a librettist’s verses are expendable once they have prompted the tune.
lenses.why: The couplet that closes the recitative rhymes taking joy with coming to an end; Auden held that opera is about people who will have their feelings at any cost.

lenses.caption: The question is che far degg’io, what must I do, and the song answers with the same verb: sempre libera degg’io, always free I must. Deggio is an old form of I must; by the dictionary the verb names an obligation and, often, a will set on something. The song states a duty she lays on herself, and its first words are always free. The English begins Let me and has no word for free. In Auden’s view a sung role commands its fate more than a spoken one, even a self-destroyer’s, and the great age of opera, Mozart’s to Verdi’s, fell in the age that believed in freedom without question.
lenses.why: The song answers her question with the question’s verb, an old must that can also express a will, and joins it to the words always free; Auden held that whoever sings commands a fate, even a self-destroyer’s.

lenses.caption: The scene has four parts: recitative, slow song, recitative, fast song, in eight, twenty-four, eight and eight lines. A short fast song to close an aria, the cabaletta, was characteristic of Italian opera in the first half of the nineteenth century. In the slow song she wonders whether he is the man she once pictured; in the fast one she chooses pleasure. Between them the libretto gives her an instant of thought, and her next word is Follie, follies; she calls the thought a vain delirium. The convention sets a fast song after the slow one; in this scene the eight lines of recitative between them are where she changes her mind.
lenses.why: The scene follows the convention of a slow song closed by a fast one, and her change of mind falls between the two: an instant of thought, one word, and the eight lines of the second recitative.

lenses.caption: Her last speech begins È strano, it is strange, and breaks off in Oh gio... ia, oh joy, the word broken in two: the two exclamations of her first speech alone in Act 1. There the strange thing was his words in her heart and the joy was being loved; here the strange thing is that the pain has stopped, and the stage direction calls her rianimata, revived. Self-deception, Auden held, cannot be sung, since what is sung is so; at most the orchestra can contradict the singer, and his example is its music as Germont comes to her deathbed, when this scene begins. Then the Doctor says È spenta, she is extinguished: a word used of flames.
lenses.why: Her last speech opens and breaks off on the two exclamations of her first speech alone, and a stage direction calls her revived; Auden held that what is sung is so and that only the orchestra can hint otherwise.

lenses.caption: Thirteen printed lines make eight lines of seven syllables by the Italian count, the measure of her slow song, rhymed like the eight lines sung to her just before. Four are shared between speakers; the first printing sets each continuation further to the right, and the marks join the pieces. In the fifth she sings ritorno a vivere, I return to living. In the sixth, her broken gio... ia, joy, is the first half and the others’ muor, she dies, the second. It stops on its last accent and rhymes with dolor, grief, the libretto’s last word. The others finish the line she breaks off, and then the stanza, in its measure and its rhymes.
lenses.why: The last lines are one stanza divided among the voices: her cry of joy and the others’ cry that she dies are the halves of one line, and the others then finish the stanza in its measure and rhymes.

ties.say: *Strange* here. For the same Italian words in Act 1 the English has *wondrous*.
Her pain. The English has *pains*, and *sorrow* in its next line.
The Italian word for joy breaks in two. The English word is whole, and it is *happiness*; in Act 1 it was *joy*.
The Italian cry asks for help for her. The English prays for her soul.

lenses.caption: The English is from the libretto published for the Metropolitan Opera House, the Italian with an English translation, in a copy printed between 1935 and 1950. It gives the first exclamation as strange here but as wondrous in Act 1, and the last as happiness where Act 1 had joy, so its reader does not meet the same words twice. Piave’s one word for her pain and the others’ grief becomes pains, sorrow and grief. Auden and Kallman wrote that in the opera house opera should be sung in its own language, and that those who want to follow should buy such a libretto and read it beforehand.
lenses.why: The English turns her two returning exclamations differently in Act 1 and Act 3, so its reader does not meet the same words twice; Auden and Kallman told operagoers to read such a libretto before the performance.

auden.says: Auden wrote that joyful, tender and noble feelings are not kept for noble characters. Everybody has them, the most depraved included. Opera can show this and spoken drama cannot, because nobody talks in song: a song can come at the wrong moment but cannot be wrong for the person who sings it.
auden.source: “Notes on Music and Opera,” in *The Dyer’s Hand* (1962), pp. 469–70
auden.checked: the scan of The Dyer’s Hand, research/auden/dh.txt, lines 22100-22119, on 2026-10-03

auden.says: In a sense, he wrote, no opera can be tragic: whatever goes wrong for its people, they are getting their own way. A singer playing a jilted bride on the point of suicide is, as every listener can tell, enjoying herself greatly.
auden.source: “Notes on Music and Opera,” in *The Dyer’s Hand* (1962), p. 468
auden.checked: the scan of The Dyer’s Hand, research/auden/dh.txt, lines 22049-22054, on 2026-10-03 (the running head of p. 468 is at line 22020)

auden.says: Music, he wrote, is by nature active: it expresses will, and a will that gives way cannot be put into song. In the same essay he says that verismo, the naturalist school of opera, exchanged the gods and princes of the old serious opera for exotic settings, the courtesans of *La Traviata* and *Manon* among them, and that these are as far from the ordinary operagoer’s life as Olympus or Versailles.
auden.checked: the scan of The Dyer’s Hand, research/auden/dh.txt, lines 22471-22477 and 22484-22492, on 2026-10-03 (the running head of p. 478 is at line 22458). The words that gloss verismo are the page's, in his own terms, read by the finisher the same day: he speaks of its theory as applied to opera (line 22484) and of a naturalist (line 22494), both on p. 478, and of its school, with the word naturalistic, on p. 480 (lines 22571-22572; the running head of p. 480 is at line 22557). He does not say realist

auden.says: A librettist’s verses, he wrote, are not written for the public. They are a letter meant for the composer alone. Their one moment comes when they prompt a melody in him, and after that they can be spared. In song, he adds, it is the syllables that cannot be spared.
auden.source: “Notes on Music and Opera,” in *The Dyer’s Hand* (1962), p. 473
auden.checked: the scan of The Dyer’s Hand, research/auden/dh.txt, lines 22261-22267 and 22286-22289, on 2026-10-03 (the running head of p. 473 is at line 22253; the poet also read lines 22242-22243 on p. 472, that the words of a song cannot be poetry, which this entry does not report, so the examiner set the page to 473)

auden.says: A play can let a mistake be found out slowly. In a libretto, he wrote, the finding out has to be abrupt, because music cannot exist where things are uncertain.
auden.quote: song cannot walk, it can only jump
auden.source: “Notes on Music and Opera,” in *The Dyer’s Hand* (1962), p. 471

auden.says: He set the great age of opera between Mozart and Verdi and tied it to an age that believed in freedom without question. For him a high C sung dead on pitch disproves the idea that chance or fate pulls the strings.
auden.source: “Notes on Music and Opera,” in *The Dyer’s Hand* (1962), p. 474

auden.says: With Chester Kallman he wrote that a translator must find the right style for each opera: the Queen of the Night, who is supernatural, cannot talk like Violetta, who is a courtesan. A translation, they add, must fit the music as it is sung, and for an aria it need give only the emotion.
auden.source: W. H. Auden and Chester Kallman, “Translating Opera Libretti,” in *The Dyer’s Hand* (1962), pp. 485, 491 and 493

sources: The text: Francesco Maria Piave, *La Traviata*, the libretto of Giuseppe Verdi’s opera, in the Italian of the libretto printed in Venice by Teresa Gattei for the first production at the Teatro La Fenice, in the season of 1852–53, as Italian Wikisource transcribes it beside a facsimile of each printed page; the passages shown here were read against those pages. The English set beside it is from [the Italian and English libretto](#/read/traviata) that Fred. Rullman of New York published for the Metropolitan Opera House. It names no translator and prints no date; the cover of the copy used names Edward Johnson as general manager of the house, which he was from 1935 to 1950.

W. H. Auden, *The Dyer’s Hand and Other Essays* (1962): “Notes on Music and Opera,” pp. 468–74; “Cav & Pag,” p. 478; “Translating Opera Libretti,” written with Chester Kallman, pp. 484–85, 488, 491, 493 and 497–98.
Alan Ansen, *The Table Talk of W. H. Auden*, edited by Nicholas Jenkins (Princeton: Ontario Review Press, 1990; London: Faber, 1991): Auden’s conversation in 1947. Not seen in full.
Abramo Basevi, *Studio sulle opere di Giuseppe Verdi* (Florence, 1859), chapter 17, on *La Traviata*, pp. 225–40.
Gustav Kobbé, *The Complete Opera Book* (New York: G. P. Putnam’s Sons, 1919), on *La Traviata*, Act 1.
*The Canadian Encyclopedia*, “Edward Johnson,” for his years as general manager of the Metropolitan Opera.

*Enciclopedia dell’Italiano* (Rome: Istituto della Enciclopedia Italiana, 2010–11), at treccani.it: Claudio Ciociola, *versificazione*, *settenario*, *rima* and *metrica e lingua*; Fabio Rossi, *melodramma, lingua del*.
*Enciclopedia Italiana* (Rome: Istituto della Enciclopedia Italiana), at treccani.it: Andrea Della Corte, *cabaletta* (1930); Mario Pelaez, *ottonario* (1935).

Treccani, *Vocabolario on line*, at treccani.it: *accendere*, *accento*, *altero*, *amore*, *anima*, *animare*, *cabaletta*, *cessare*, *croce*, *cuore*, *delizia*, *dolore*, *dovere*, *finire*, *folleggiare*, *gioia*, *gioire*, *insolito*, *lauda*, *libero*, *palpito*, *rianimare*, *rinascere*, *rio*, *scolpire*, *soccorrere*, *solingo*, *spegnere*, *strano*, *trasalire*, *trasvolare*, *traviare*, *tumulto*, *vigore*, *voluttà*, *vortice* and the other words glossed. The words as sung: *Verdi’s Opera La Traviata*, containing the Italian text, with an English translation, and the music of all the principal airs (Boston: Oliver Ditson), and the Italian column of the Rullman libretto.

H. G. Liddell and R. Scott, *A Greek-English Lexicon*, revised by H. S. Jones (Oxford, 1940), at the Perseus Digital Library, under *antilabe*; “Antilabe,” in Wikipedia: the name of a line of verse shared between speakers.
caveats: Auden wrote no essay on *La Traviata*. The view given here is his general account of opera, from pages where this opera is one of his examples; fitting it to these passages is this page’s doing. That he called the opera a great work is known at second hand.

The Italian is the libretto as first printed for Venice, in a transcription that differs from the page in a few marks of punctuation and spells out the speakers’ names. As sung, to judge by old librettos, the fast song has other words in six lines, and Alfredo sings *palpito*.
The English is an old libretto version by an unnamed translator. It is free, and in the fast song it follows the words as sung, not the lines shown beside it.

Syllables are counted by the Italian rules, and the stresses marked are one reader’s. Three of the last lines of the opera count as lines of seven only if the vowel that ends one speaker’s words runs into the vowel that begins the next speaker’s.

The return of Alfredo’s tune in Violetta’s song is reported from Abramo Basevi’s study of 1859 and Gustav Kobbé’s opera guide of 1919; no score was seen. *Antilabe* is a term of Greek drama, taken here from a Greek lexicon; no handbook of Italian verse was found that uses it.
open: Ansen's Table Talk was not seen: the remark that La Traviata is a great work, and the date 1947, rest on the research notes (snippets, no page).

No score was seen. What the music does (the return of Alfredo's phrase in the andantino, the tenor's voice behind the scenes after the fast song) is reported from Basevi (1859), read in a machine-read scan whose page numbers I took from the running heads (the OCR prints 234 as "23i").

The sung words of the fast song, and Alfredo's palpito, were read in American librettos that print the words under the music or beside the English (Ditson; Samuel French; Rullman's Italian column), not in a score. Who changed Piave's words, and when, I did not find. Nine Italian printings of 1856 to 1881 at archive.org (six of them Ricordi's, two of Naples, one of Genoa), read in their machine-read text, keep the words shown here, in the fast song and in Alfredo's line.

The Wikisource index dates the printed libretto 1852 and the work page 1853; the title page calls the opera written for La Fenice, to be given in the Carnival and Lent season of 1852-53. The page says only "as first printed" and "for the first production".

The translator of the hosted English is unknown. That it follows the sung words in the fast song is an inference from Rullman's own Italian column, which has the sung words, and from its second line; its fifth line could come from either text. Whether it was ever sung is not known, and the page does not say so.

That the last thirteen printed lines are eight lines of verse is shown by the first printing, which sets the pieces of each divided line in steps (page images of pp. 34 and 35, seen). That each of the eight is a seven is my count. It needs the run of vowel into vowel across a change of speaker in three lines and, in the seventh, the one-syllable reading of the first two vowels of the heroine's name; the regular stanza pattern and a line of eleven shared the same way earlier in the scene support it, and no source was found that says it of this passage.

In the last line the first printing sets two small words one over the other (page image of p. 35, seen); the transcription gives the lower one in brackets. Who sings which the libretto does not say: its margin gives the line to all. The Ditson libretto heads the line "Alfredo e Tutti", and the hosted English has two cries, Alfred's and everyone's. The note on the word says only what is printed and that the English makes two cries.

Plate 3 shows whole rows of the Italian cut, in which speakers' names and stage directions stand inside the row (notes.md has the word numbers); the artist may want to set them apart. The first printing has the names in the margin, shortened (Vio., Alf., Dot.); the transcription spells them out. The cut text breaks her last speech into two blocks at a blank line of the transcription, which is the turn from p. 34 to p. 35 of the printing, so the page will set a little space after row 1.4; it is not a stanza break. The English beside it will carry its speakers' names over the speeches and has one speech more than the Italian: two cries at the end where the Italian prints one line.

The transcription differs from the first printing at three places in the rows shown, all punctuation (page images of pp. 10 and 11, seen): row 9.0 word 6 ends in an exclamation mark where the print has a question mark; row 5.2 has a comma after word 0 that the print lacks; row 10.4 ends in a comma that the print lacks. The text cannot be mended without retyping it, so the second caveat and the note on row 9.0 tell the reader.

Row 10.7 is cut after word 5 to leave the stage direction out of the scansion, so the page will set points of omission after the last line of the fast song. In plate 1 the page will set a little space before each return of the four lines (they are blocks of their own in the cut); the first printing sets them off too, by a deeper indent, and sets Alfredo's eight lines as two groups of four.

The record on the site (the fast song, 1919) was not listened to; it will have the sung words, not the lines shown. The record's note on the page now says so (the lead, notes.md, The lead before the finisher).

Auden's sentence about song that can only jump is said of the discovery of a mistake. The page used to apply it to the turn between the two songs (the Scene caption of the second passage) and to the last lines (the Shared caption of the third). The finisher took it out of both on 2026-10-03: on p. 471 a mistake is a false belief that the plot later shows to be false, self-deception is one kind of it, the kind opera cannot use, and nothing on the page fits the sentence to these lines. It now stands only in the list under More from Auden, with its quotation.

From the examiner: in the third passage the page sets each stage direction of the English libretto under the name of the next speaker (Reviving under ALL, the direction about her pulse under ALFRED). The build hands a direction to the row that follows it, and the page prints that row's speaker first. In this libretto each direction follows the speech it belongs to. The label over the English column used to say the directions were left out, which was false on the page; it now says each direction goes with the speech above it. The order itself can only be mended in the kit: build/pieces.mjs where a pair row gets its `dir`, and site/js/kit/plate.js where `who` is printed before `dir`.

From the examiner: in the first and second passages the page prints the English libretto's headings of the two songs (the lines that begin Scene and Air) as stage directions. In the first passage that heading stands after the points of omission and just before the four returning lines, though the seven lines left out come after it in the libretto.

From the examiner: the name antilabe now stands on Liddell and Scott's lexicon (in dramatic dialogue, the division of a line between two speakers), with Wikipedia for the rest. It is a term of Greek drama. No Italian handbook was found that uses it of a libretto, and the last caveat says so.

From the examiner: the return of Alfredo's tune in her slow song now has a second witness, Gustav Kobbé's Complete Opera Book (1919), which calls it a refrain. I recall, and could not source here, that the orchestra plays the same tune under her last speech in Act 3. Basevi and Kobbé do not say so and no score was seen, so the page does not say it. If a score or a study can be opened, it would tie the third passage to the first.

From the examiner: the tab English of the third passage no longer cites Auden on syllables (p. 473), which the poet gave as a reason of another kind. It now cites what he and Kallman say on p. 484: opera houses should give opera in its own language, and whoever wants to follow should buy a libretto with an English version and read it first. The English shown is from such a libretto. That Auden ever held this one in his hands is not known and is not said.

From the examiner: the hosted English libretto prints no date, but the cover of the scanned copy names Edward Johnson as general manager of the Metropolitan Opera House, and he held that post from May 1935 to 1950 (The Canadian Encyclopedia; Wikipedia). So this copy was printed in those years, which take in the year of the course. The tab English of the third passage and the first entry of the sources now say so; the note of the hosted text (site/data/texts/traviata/index.json) still says only that it gives no date, and its `year` is empty. The translation itself may be older and its maker is still unknown; the library's shelf label on the binding reads 1900. The Internet Archive's record reports no notice of copyright in the copy.

From the examiner: besides the three marks of punctuation listed above, the transcription differs from the first printing in one word of line 301 and one of line 284 of the Italian file (page image of p. 10, seen). Neither line is shown, and neither difference changes the count of syllables.

From the examiner: on p. 493 Auden and Kallman follow their sentence on what the translation of an aria must do with another: the arias are an opera's high points, so the quality of a translation matters most there. The tab English of the first passage reports the first sentence and their warning about rhymes of two syllables, and not the second sentence.
